tweets: A handful of painters walked out of a crumbling Mughal court into the Himalayan foothills, and turned Krishna's love story into the tenderest paintings India ever made.
This was Pahari painting, a style born in tiny hill kingdoms like Basohli, Guler, Jasrota, Chamba, Mandi and Kangra, spread across today's Himachal Pradesh and Jammu, from the 1600s to the 1800s.

Its masters were often one family. Pandit Seu's sons Manaku and Nainsukh carried Mughal-trained naturalism into the hills. Nainsukh (c.1710-1778) painted courtly life with a precision rare for his time.

The style peaked at Kangra under Raja Sansar Chand (r.1775-1823). Artists illustrated the Bhagavata Purana and Jayadeva's Gita Govinda: Radha and Krishna amid monsoon clouds, rivers, and lush green valleys.

No gold, no grandeur, just love painted in whispers. Centuries later, these palm-sized works still read like poetry. Follow @yddoseOfHistory for your daily dose of history.
